  1. 1 Must see within Kita

    Umeda Sky Building — Kuchū Teien Floating Garden Observatory

    The 173 m twin-tower skyscraper (1993) joined at the top by the open-air Floating Garden observation deck — 360° views over Osaka, open till 22:30.

    Look for observation deck

    Umeda Sky Building, northwest of JR Osaka Station, Kita-ku, Osaka, Japan

    Recommended by , ,

  2. 2 Must see within Kita

    LUCUA Characters World — Pokémon Center Osaka & Nintendo OSAKA

    Osaka's answer to Tokyo's Character Street: LUCUA SOUTH opened 5 April 2026 and gathered Pokémon Center Osaka, Nintendo OSAKA and the ONE PIECE Mugiwara Store (moved from Daimaru Umeda) on its top floors, growing to 30+ character shops (Sanrio, Square Enix, Minecraft) by autumn 2026.

    Look for ★ Anime & pop culture — Pokémon · Nintendo (Mario, Zelda, Splatoon) · One Piece — Kansai's biggest official character-store cluster, the Pokémon Center and Nintendo flagship stores of western Japan · character shops, pop culture

    LUCUA SOUTH 10–13F (South Gate Building), JR Osaka Station, Umeda, Kita-ku, Osaka

    Recommended by , ,

    Nakanoshima Museum of Art, Osaka

    The city art museum that opened on Nakanoshima in February 2022 — modern and contemporary art and design, part of the island's museum cluster.

  8. 8 Worth the detour within Kita

    Osaka City Central Public Hall (Nakanoshima)

    Neo-Renaissance red-brick hall completed 1918 with a donation from stockbroker Einosuke Iwamoto (design Tatsuno Kingo & Okada Shin'ichirō); restored 1999–2002 and designated an Important Cultural Property in 2002. Free basement history exhibit.

    Look for historic architecture

    Nakanoshima, Kita-ku, Osaka

    Recommended by , ,

  9. 9 Worth the detour within Kita

    Tsuyu no Tenjinsha (Ohatsu Tenjin)

    1,300-year-old Umeda shrine named for Sugawara no Michizane's dew-and-tears poem; nicknamed after Ohatsu, heroine of Chikamatsu's 1703 'Love Suicides at Sonezaki', set in its grove — now a matchmaking power spot.

    Look for shrine

    Sonezaki, Kita-ku, Osaka

    Recommended by , ,

    Temma's shrine to Sugawara no Michizane, god of learning, at the head of Tenjinbashi-suji; home of the Tenjin Matsuri.

    Temma, Kita-ku, Osaka, Japan

    Tenjinbashi 6-chōme, Kita-ku, Osaka, Japan

How we choose

Every place is recommended by named sources (Yelp and TripAdvisor never count as the recommender), pinned to its door from a published coordinate, and status-checked. Closed places stay, flagged, so you know they’re gone.

Must see
The places to plan a visit around — graded within each area, not across the city.
Worth the detour
Strong picks, worth going out of your way for.
Deep cut
For the curious: smaller, odder, more local.

Within each area, places are ordered by tier, then by number of named sources — never by popularity. Numbers on the cards match the pins on the map. No ratings, prices or opening hours are shown, because the guide doesn’t hold verified ones.

159 sights and 210 places to eat across Osaka — the city of kuidaore, eat till you drop — every one traceable to its source: okonomiyaki teppan, kushikatsu counters, Michelin Bib Gourmand udon and soba, Kita and Minami, the castle, the bay and the Kansai ring.

How this guide was made

How the cuisine filters were policed

Every food card names a specific dish — a label alone doesn’t qualify. A cuisine tag names the kitchen’s own tradition, never one dish it serves. Tabelog and Retty scores may measure popularity but never count as a source.

Web-searched in Japanese and English, fact-checked

Every place is traceable to two credible sources, or a lone Michelin / UNESCO / Agency for Cultural Affairs designation — recorded in data/sources.json. Every coordinate is verified into data/geocodes.json and every place status-checked open. Yelp/TripAdvisor/Tabelog never count toward the two-source bar.
